en: Parivāra 15.
Mahāsaṅgāma 1.
What Should Be Known by One Who Is Speaking, etc.
A monk who dwells in the midst of the battle and speaks within the Saṅgha must know the matter, he must know the failure, he must know the offense,
he must know the source, he must know the mode, he must know the sequence, he must know what has been done and what has not been done,
he must know the formal act, he must know the legal issue, he must know the means of settlement, and he must not follow a course of favoritism.
One should proceed; one should not proceed with a course of hatred, nor with a course of delusion, nor with a course of fear.

One should convince [the other] at a point where conviction is possible; one should inspire [them] at a point where inspiration is possible; one should look upon [them] at a point where looking is possible;
one should instill confidence at a point where confidence is possible. Thinking, "I have gained a following," one should not despise the opposing side. Thinking, "I am learned..."
One who has heard little should not be despised; one who is more senior should not be despised because one is younger;
one should not speak out regarding what has not been brought forward; when a matter has been brought forward, it should not be neglected according to the Dhamma and the Vinaya.
Whatever Dhamma, whatever Vinaya, and whatever teaching of the Teacher there is by which that legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) is settled—that is how that legal issue should be settled.
"The subject matter must be known":
the subject matter of the eight *pārājika* rules must be known; the subject matter of the twenty-three *saṅghādisesa* rules must be known; the subject matter of the two *aniyata* rules must be known;
the subject matter of the forty-two *nissaggiya pācittiya* rules must be known; and the subject matter of the one hundred and eighty-eight *pācittiya* rules must be known.
The basis for the offenses must be known; the basis for the twelve *pāṭidesanīya* offenses must be known; the basis for the *dukkaṭa* offenses must be known;
the basis for the *dubbhāsita* offenses must be known.
"Failure must be known" means:
Failure in virtue is to be known; failure in conduct is to be known; failure in view is to be known; failure in livelihood is to be known.

"Offense is to be known" means that an offense involving defeat (pārājika) is to be known, an offense of formal meeting (saṅghādisesa) is to be known, and a grave offense (thullaccaya) is to be known.

An offense entailing expiation (pācittiya) must be known; an offense entailing acknowledgment (pāṭidesanīya) must be known; an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) must be known; an offense of improper speech (dubbhāsita) must be known.

"The origin must be known" means that the origin of the eight rules on defeat (pārājika) must be known; the origin of the twenty-three rules on formal meeting (saṅghādisesa) must be known; the origin of the two undetermined rules (aniyata) must be known...

The origin must be known: the origin of the forty-two offenses entailing relinquishment (nissaggiya) must be known; the origin of the one hundred and eighty-eight offenses entailing expiation (pācittiya) must be known;
the origin of the twelve offenses entailing acknowledgment (pāṭidesanīya) must be known; the origin of the offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) must be known;
the origin of the offenses of improper speech (dubbhāsita) must be known.

"The manner must be known" means: the Saṅgha must be known by its manner; the group must be known by its manner; the individual must be known by his manner; the accuser must be known by his manner; the accused must be known by his manner.
"The Saṅgha must be known by its manner" means:

"Is this Saṅgha capable of settling this legal issue in accordance with the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction, or is it not?"—in this way the Saṅgha is to be known by its characteristics.
"The group is to be known by its characteristics":

"Is this group capable of settling this legal issue in accordance with the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction, or is it not?"—in this way the group is to be known by its characteristics.
"A person is to be known by their manner":

one should consider whether this person is capable of settling this legal issue in accordance with the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction, or not; in this way, a person is to be known by their manner.
"The accuser is to be known by their manner."
"Does this venerable one reprove another while being established in five qualities, or not?"— in this way the reprover is to be known by his characteristics.
"Is this venerable one reproved while being established in two qualities, namely truth and imperturbability, or not?"— in this way the reproved is to be known by his characteristics.
"One must understand the sequence of before and after":

does this venerable one perhaps transfer from one basis to another basis, from one failure to another failure, or from one offense to another offense; or does he deny what he has admitted, or admit what he has denied?
Or whether one evades one thing with another— thus the sequence of what precedes and what follows must be understood.

"What has been done and what has not been done must be understood" means that sexual intercourse must be understood, the preliminary to sexual intercourse must be understood, and the stage preceding sexual intercourse must be understood.
"The nature of sexual intercourse is to be known" means that the mutual penetration of the two organs is to be known.
"The preliminary stage of sexual intercourse is to be known" means...
A bhikkhu takes another’s genitals with his own mouth.
One should know the preliminary stages of sexual intercourse:
praise and blame, physical contact, lewd speech, service according to one’s desire, and the offering of words.
"Kamma should be known":
the sixteen types of kamma should be known—
four *apalokana*-kammāni should be known, four *ñatti*-kammāni should be known, four *ñattidutiya*-kammāni should be known, and four *ñatticatuttha*-kammāni should be known.
"Legal issues are to be known":
four legal issues are to be known—

the legal issue arising from a dispute is to be known, the legal issue arising from an accusation is to be known, the legal issue arising from an offense is to be known, and the legal issue arising from business is to be known.
"Samatha (settling) should be understood": seven kinds of samatha should be understood—

sammukhāvinaya (settlement in the presence of) should be understood, sativinaya (settlement by recollection) should be understood, amūḷhavinaya (settlement for one who is no longer insane) should be understood, paṭiññātakaraṇa (acting according to what has been admitted) should be understood, yebhuyyasikā (decision by majority) should be understood, tassapāpiyasikā (reprimand for being worse) should be understood, and tiṇavatthāraka (covering over as with grass) should be understood.
2. One Should Not Go by Way of Bias.
Regarding the statement "one should not go by way of bias":
how does one who goes by way of bias go by way of bias?
In this case, someone— thinking, “This is my preceptor, or teacher, or co-resident, or pupil, or one who shares a preceptor with me, or one who shares a teacher with me, or one seen by me,
or one with whom I am intimate, or a kinsman”— out of compassion for him and out of a desire to protect him,
proclaims what is non-Dhamma as Dhamma, and what is Dhamma as non-Dhamma, and what is non-discipline as discipline.
He illuminates what is discipline as non-discipline; he illuminates what was not spoken nor uttered by the Tathāgata as having been spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata;
he illuminates what was spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata as not having been spoken nor uttered by the Tathāgata;
he illuminates what was not practiced by the Tathāgata as having been practiced by the Tathāgata; he illuminates what was practiced by the Tathāgata as not having been practiced by the Tathāgata.
He proclaims what was not laid down by the Tathāgata as having been laid down by the Tathāgata;
he proclaims what was laid down by the Tathāgata as not having been laid down by the Tathāgata; he proclaims a non-offense as an offense; he proclaims an offense as a non-offense;
he proclaims a light offense as a heavy offense; he proclaims a heavy offense as a light offense.
He proclaims a remaining offense as one without remainder; he proclaims an offense without remainder as one with remainder;
he proclaims a grave offense as one that is not grave; he proclaims an offense that is not grave as one that is grave.
By these eighteen grounds, one who proceeds through favoritism acts for the harm of many people, for the unhappiness of many people, for the ruin, harm, and suffering of gods and humans.
By proceeding with favoritism through these eighteen grounds, one maintains oneself wounded and mangled; one becomes blameworthy and subject to censure by the wise, and generates much demerit.
One who proceeds with favoritism proceeds in this manner. "One should not proceed with hostility"—thus it is said.
How does one going toward the wrong course of hatred go toward that wrong course?
Here, someone conceives resentment, thinking: "He has done me harm"; he conceives resentment, thinking: "He is doing me harm"; he conceives resentment, thinking: "He will do me harm";
or he conceives resentment, thinking: "He has done harm to one who is dear and pleasing to me" ... "he is doing harm" ... "he will do harm."
"He has acted for my harm... he will act for my harm"—thus one harbors resentment. "He has acted for the benefit of one who is disagreeable and unpleasant to me...
he is acting for their benefit... he will act for their benefit"—thus one harbors resentment.
Through these nine grounds for resentment, being resentful, hostile, angry, and overcome by anger, one proclaims what is non-Dhamma as Dhamma, and what is Dhamma as non-Dhamma... [and so forth].
He proclaims a grave offense as a non-grave offense, and he proclaims a non-grave offense as a grave offense.

By proceeding through these eighteen grounds with a mistaken course due to malice, he acts for the harm of many people, for the unhappiness of many people, for the ruin, harm, and suffering of many people, including both gods and humans.

By proceeding through these eighteen grounds with a mistaken course due to malice, he maintains himself in a state of injury and affliction; he is blameworthy and subject to reproach by the wise, and he generates much demerit.
One who goes toward hatred goes toward hatred in this way.
How does one who goes toward delusion go toward delusion when it should not be gone toward as delusion?
One who is lustful proceeds by way of lust; one who is corrupt proceeds by way of hatred; one who is deluded proceeds by way of delusion;

one who is misapprehending proceeds by way of wrong view. Deluded, utterly bewildered, and overcome by delusion, he proclaims what is non-Dhamma as Dhamma, and what is Dhamma as non-Dhamma... [and so on].
He proclaims a grave offense as a non-grave offense, and he proclaims a non-grave offense as a grave offense.

By proceeding through these eighteen grounds with a course based on delusion, he acts for the harm of many people, for the unhappiness of many people, for the ruin, harm, and suffering of many people, including both gods and humans.

By proceeding through these eighteen grounds with a course based on delusion, he maintains himself in a state of injury and impairment; he becomes blameworthy and subject to reproach by the wise, and he generates much demerit.
One who goes to a state of delusion goes to that state of delusion in this way.
How does one who goes to a state of fear— thinking, "one should not go to a state of fear"— go to that state of fear?
In this case, someone— thinking, “This person relies on the uneven, or relies on thickets, or relies on the powerful; he is harsh and cruel,
and will cause an obstacle to my life or an obstacle to my holy life”—
out of fear of him proclaims what is non-Dhamma as Dhamma, what is Dhamma as non-Dhamma, what is non-discipline as discipline, and what is discipline as non-discipline.
He illuminates what was not spoken or uttered by the Tathāgata as having been spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata;
he illuminates what was spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata as not having been spoken or uttered by the Tathāgata;
he illuminates what was not practiced by the Tathāgata as having been practiced by the Tathāgata; he illuminates what was practiced by the Tathāgata as not having been practiced by the Tathāgata.
He proclaims what was not laid down by the Tathāgata as having been laid down by the Tathāgata; he proclaims what was laid down by the Tathāgata as not having been laid down by the Tathāgata;
he proclaims a non-offense as an offense; he proclaims an offense as a non-offense;
he proclaims a light offense as a heavy offense; he proclaims a heavy offense as a light offense; [he proclaims] what has a remainder...
He explains a non-residual offense as a residual offense; he explains a residual offense as a non-residual offense;
he explains a grave offense as a non-grave offense; he explains a non-grave offense as a grave offense.

By these eighteen grounds, one who proceeds with fear-based deviation acts for the harm of many people, for the unhappiness of many people, for the detriment, harm, and suffering of many people, including both devas and humans.

Proceeding by way of fear on these eighteen grounds, one maintains oneself in a state of being wounded and injured; one becomes blameworthy and subject to censure by the wise, and generates much demerit.
One who proceeds by way of fear proceeds thus: out of desire, out of hatred, out of fear, and out of delusion.
He who transgresses the Dhamma—
his fame diminishes,
like the moon in the dark fortnight.
3. Discourse on Wrong Course and Right Course. How does one not go astray through favoritism?
By pointing out what is non-Dhamma as "non-Dhamma," one does not go astray through favoritism; by pointing out what is Dhamma as "Dhamma," one does not go astray through favoritism.

He does not proceed by way of favoritism when demonstrating that what is non-discipline is non-discipline; he does not proceed by way of favoritism when demonstrating that what is discipline is discipline;
he does not proceed by way of favoritism when demonstrating that what was neither spoken nor uttered by the Tathāgata was neither spoken nor uttered by the Tathāgata;
and he does not proceed by way of favoritism when demonstrating that what was spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata was spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata.

When illuminating [a practice], he does not fall into bias through desire; when illuminating that which was not practiced by the Tathāgata as "not practiced by the Tathāgata," he does not fall into bias through desire;
when illuminating that which was practiced by the Tathāgata as "practiced by the Tathāgata," he does not fall into bias through desire;
when illuminating that which was not prescribed by the Tathāgata as "not prescribed by the Tathāgata," he does not fall into bias through desire.
He does not proceed by way of favoritism when demonstrating what was prescribed by the Tathāgata as "prescribed by the Tathāgata";
he does not proceed by way of favoritism when demonstrating a non-offense as "a non-offense";
he does not proceed by way of favoritism when demonstrating an offense as "an offense"; and he does not proceed by way of favoritism when demonstrating a light offense as "a light offense."
When he explains a grave offense as a grave offense, he does not fall into partiality;

when he explains an offense with remainder as an offense with remainder, he does not fall into partiality; when he explains an offense without remainder as an offense without remainder, he does not fall into partiality;
when he explains a gross offense as a gross offense, he does not [fall into partiality].
One does not fall into bias through desire when one points out a non-grave offense as a non-grave offense;
thus one does not fall into bias through desire.
How does one not fall into bias through hatred?
When one points out what is non-Dhamma as "non-Dhamma," one does not go to a wrong course; when one points out what is Dhamma as "Dhamma," one does not go to a wrong course...

[and so on] ...when one points out a grave offense as "a grave offense," one does not go to a wrong course; when one points out a minor offense as "a minor offense," one does not go to a wrong course.
In this way, one does not go to a wrong course.
How does one not go to a state of delusion?
By explaining what is non-Dhamma as "non-Dhamma," one does not go to a state of delusion; by explaining what is Dhamma as "Dhamma," one does not go to a state of delusion...

[and so on] ...by explaining a grave offense as "a grave offense," one does not go to a state of delusion; by explaining a non-grave offense as "a non-grave offense," one does not go to a state of delusion.
Thus he does not go by way of delusion.
How does he not go by way of fear?
When he proclaims what is non-Dhamma as "non-Dhamma," he does not go by way of fear; when he proclaims what is Dhamma as "Dhamma," he does not go by way of fear.
He proceeds; when demonstrating what is non-discipline as "non-discipline," he does not proceed out of fear; when demonstrating what is discipline as "discipline," he does not proceed out of fear;
when demonstrating what was not spoken or uttered by the Tathāgata as "not spoken or uttered by the Tathāgata," he does not proceed out of fear;
and when demonstrating what was spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata as "spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata," [he does not proceed out of fear].

When illuminating [the Dhamma], one does not go to a state of fear; when illuminating that which was not practiced by the Tathāgata as "not practiced by the Tathāgata," one does not go to a state of fear;
when illuminating that which was practiced by the Tathāgata as "practiced by the Tathāgata," one does not go to a state of fear;
when illuminating that which was not prescribed by the Tathāgata as "not prescribed by the Tathāgata," one does not go to a state of fear.
When declaring, "It has been prescribed by the Tathāgata; it has been prescribed by the Tathāgata," one does not go along a path of fear;
when declaring, "A non-offense is a non-offense," one does not go along a path of fear; when declaring, "An offense is an offense," one does not go along a path of fear;
when declaring, "A light offense is a light offense," one does not go along a path of fear; [when declaring,] "A grave offense..."
When explaining a grave offense as a grave offense, one does not go astray out of fear;

when explaining an offense with remainder as an offense with remainder, one does not go astray out of fear; when explaining an offense without remainder as an offense without remainder, one does not go astray out of fear;
when explaining a gross offense as a gross offense, one does not go astray out of fear.
When one goes, explaining a non-gross offense as a non-gross offense, one does not go by way of fear.
Thus one does not go by way of fear. [One does not go] out of desire, hatred, fear, or delusion.
He who does not transgress the Dhamma—
his fame increases,
like the moon during the waxing fortnight.
4. Discussion on Persuasion, etc.
How does one persuade in a matter that requires persuasion?

By pointing out what is non-Dhamma as "non-Dhamma," one persuades in a matter that requires persuasion; by pointing out what is Dhamma as "Dhamma," one persuades in a matter that requires persuasion … [and so forth] …

When one explains a grave offense as a grave offense, one persuades [the person] at a point where persuasion is appropriate; when one explains a non-grave offense as a non-grave offense, one persuades [the person] at a point where persuasion is appropriate.
This is how one persuades at a point where persuasion is appropriate.
How does one cause [the person] to reflect at a point where reflection is appropriate?

When one explains what is contrary to the Dhamma as "contrary to the Dhamma," one causes [the person] to reflect upon a matter that should be reflected upon; when one explains what is the Dhamma as "the Dhamma," one causes [the person] to reflect upon a matter that should be reflected upon...

pe ...when one explains a grave offense as "a grave offense," one causes [the person] to reflect upon a matter that should be reflected upon; when one explains a non-grave offense as "a non-grave offense," one causes [the person] to reflect upon a matter that should be reflected upon.
In this way, one causes [the person] to reflect upon a matter that should be reflected upon.
How does one look upon what ought to be looked upon?
One looks upon what ought to be looked upon by pointing out that what is non-Dhamma is non-Dhamma; one looks upon what ought to be looked upon by pointing out that what is Dhamma is Dhamma...

[and so on] ...one looks upon what ought to be looked upon by pointing out that a grave offense is a grave offense; one looks upon what ought to be looked upon by pointing out that a non-grave offense is a non-grave offense.
Thus he looks upon what is to be looked upon.
How does he inspire confidence in what inspires confidence?

By pointing out that what is non-Dhamma is non-Dhamma, he inspires confidence in what inspires confidence; by pointing out that what is Dhamma is Dhamma, he inspires confidence in what inspires confidence... [and so on].

When one describes a grave offense as a grave offense, one inspires confidence in a matter that inspires confidence; when one describes a non-grave offense as a non-grave offense, one inspires confidence in a matter that inspires confidence.
In this way, one inspires confidence in a matter that inspires confidence.
5. Disparaging the Opposing Side, etc.
How does one who has gained a faction despise the opposing faction?
In this case, someone has gained a faction, gained a retinue, possesses a following, and is proud of his kin.

Thinking, “This person has not gained a faction, has not gained a retinue, has no following, and is not proud of his kin,” he despises him and proclaims what is non-Dhamma as Dhamma, and what is Dhamma as non-Dhamma... [and so forth].
He proclaims a grave offense as a non-grave offense, and he proclaims a non-grave offense as a grave offense.
Thinking, "I have gained a following," he despises the faction of others.
How does he despise one who has heard little, thinking, "I am learned"?
Here, someone is learned, possessing what he has heard, and a repository of what he has heard.
Disregarding another because of thinking, "This one is of little learning, of little tradition, and of little retention," he proclaims non-Dhamma as Dhamma, and Dhamma as non-Dhamma...
[and so on] ...he proclaims a grave offense as a minor offense, and a minor offense as a grave offense.
Thus, thinking "I am one who has heard much," one despises one who has heard little.
How does one despise a junior by thinking "I am more senior"?
Here, a certain elder is of long standing, having gone forth for a long time; [thinking] "This person is a newcomer, unknown, and of little experience..."
Thinking, “My word will not be done,” he, out of contempt for him, proclaims what is non-Dhamma as Dhamma, and what is Dhamma as non-Dhamma...
[and so on] ...he proclaims a grave offense as a minor offense, and a minor offense as a grave offense.
Thinking, “I am more senior,” he treats one who is junior with contempt.
"One should not speak of what has not arrived" means that a burden not yet crossed over should not be brought across.
"What has arrived should not be neglected according to the Dhamma and the Vinaya."
Whatever matter for which the Saṅgha has assembled, that matter must not be neglected in accordance with the Dhamma and the Vinaya.
"By means of the Dhamma" means by means of the factual basis.
"By which discipline" means having accused and reminded [the offender].
"By which teaching of the Teacher" means...

Through the perfection of the motion and the perfection of the proclamation; by whatever Dhamma, by whatever Vinaya, and by whatever Teacher’s instruction that legal issue is settled, in that manner should that legal issue be settled.
6. Examination of the Investigator:
The investigator should question the accuser—

“Friend, when you suspended the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) of this bhikkhu, on account of what did you suspend it? Did you suspend it on account of a failure in virtue (*sīlavipatti*), or did you suspend it on account of a failure in conduct (*ācāravipatti*), or did you suspend it on account of a failure in view (*diṭṭhivipatti*)?
If he should say, “I suspend it on account of a failure in virtue, or I suspend it on account of a failure in conduct, or I suspend it on account of a failure in view,” he should be addressed thus:
“Does the venerable one know failure in virtue, know failure in conduct, and know failure in view?
If he should say, “Friends,
I do indeed know failure in virtue, I know failure in conduct, and I know failure in view,” he should be addressed as follows:
“But what, friends, is failure in virtue, what is failure in conduct, and what is failure in view?
If he should say this:
“The four offenses entailing expulsion and the thirteen offenses requiring formal meeting of the Saṅgha—this is failure in virtue.”
“Thullaccaya, pācittiya, pāṭidesanīya, dukkaṭa, and dubbhāsita—this is failure in conduct.
Wrong view and extremist views—this is failure in view. To him it should be said:
“Friend, when you suspended this bhikkhu’s invitation ceremony, did you suspend it on account of what was seen, or on account of what was heard, or on account of suspicion?”

If he should say, "I set aside the invitation on account of what has been seen, or I set it aside on account of what has been heard, or I set it aside on account of suspicion," he should be addressed thus:
"Friend, as for the fact that you have set aside this bhikkhu’s invitation on account of what has been seen, what have you seen?"
How was it seen by you? When was it seen by you? Where was it seen by you? Was he seen committing an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika)?
Was he seen committing an offense entailing suspension from the Saṅgha (saṅghādisesa)? [Was he seen committing] a grave offense (thullaccaya) ...
an offense entailing confession (pācittiya) ...?

“While you were seen committing an offense entailing confession, an offense of wrong-doing, or an offense of improper speech, where were you, where was this monk, what were you doing, and what was this monk doing?”
If he should say this:

“Friend, it is not on account of what has been seen that I suspend the invitation ceremony for this bhikkhu; rather, it is on account of what has been heard that I suspend the invitation ceremony,” he should be addressed thus:
“Friend, as for the fact that you suspend the invitation ceremony for this bhikkhu on account of what has been heard, what have you heard? How was it heard?”
"You have heard it; when did you hear it? Where did you hear it? You have heard that he has committed a *pārājika* offense; you have heard that he has committed a *saṅghādisesa* offense;
[you have heard that he has committed] a *thullaccaya*...
a *pācittiya*..."

"I have heard that he has committed an offense entailing confession (pāṭidesanīya), a wrong-doing (dukkaṭa), or an ill-spoken act (dubbhāsita); it was heard by a bhikkhu, heard by a bhikkhunī, or heard by a female trainee (sikkhamānā)."
“Was it heard by a novice monk, was it heard by a novice nun, was it heard by a lay male follower, was it heard by a lay female follower,
was it heard by kings, was it heard by royal ministers, was it heard by members of other sects, or was it heard by disciples of other sects? If he should say this:
“I do not, friend, suspend the invitation ceremony for this monk because of what I have heard; rather, I suspend the invitation ceremony because of suspicion. He should be addressed thus:
“Friend, as for the fact that you suspend the invitation ceremony for this monk because of suspicion, what do you suspect?
How do you suspect? When did you suspect? Where did you suspect? Do you suspect that he has committed an offense entailing expulsion?”
If you suspect that he has committed a *saṅghādisesa* offense, [you incur] a *thullaccaya*...
a *pācittiya*...
a *pāṭidesanīya*...

If you suspect that he has committed an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) … or an offense of wrong speech (dubbhāsita), and you suspect this after hearing it from a bhikkhu, or after hearing it from a bhikkhunī,
or after hearing it from a female trainee (sikkhamānā), or after hearing it from a male novice (sāmaṇera), or after hearing it from a female novice (sāmaṇerī).
“Do you suspect it because you have heard it from a lay follower? Do you suspect it because you have heard it from a female lay follower? Do you suspect it because you have heard it from kings?
Do you suspect it because you have heard it from royal ministers? Do you suspect it because you have heard it from members of other sects?
Or do you suspect it because you have heard it from the disciples of those other sects?”
What is seen accords with what is seen;
what is seen meets with what is seen.
Dependent on what is seen, it does not arise.
One who is suspected of being impure:
that person’s invitation ceremony (pavāraṇā) must be performed upon his own admission.
What has been heard accords with what has been heard;
what has been heard harmonizes with what has been heard.
One does not go beyond what has been heard.
One who is suspected of being impure:
that person’s invitation (pavāraṇā) should be performed by means of his own admission.
The known accords with the known;
the known flows together with the known;
one does not go beyond the known.
A person suspected of being impure should be dealt with by means of a formal admission; by him,
the invitation ceremony (pavāraṇā) must be performed.
7. Analysis of Questions (Pucchāvibhāga) "What have you seen?"—what kind of question is this?
"In what way have you seen it?"—what kind of question is this?
"What have you seen?"—what kind of question is this?
"Where have you seen it?"—what kind of question is this? "What is it that you have seen?"—what kind of question is this?
There are four kinds of questions: questions concerning the basis, questions concerning failure, questions concerning offenses, and questions concerning transgression.

"Questions concerning the basis" refers to questions concerning the basis for the eight *pārājika* rules, questions concerning the basis for the twenty-three *saṅghādisesa* rules, and [questions concerning] the two undetermined rules.

Inquiries concerning the bases: inquiries concerning the forty-two offenses entailing relinquishment (*nissaggiya*), inquiries concerning the one hundred and eighty-eight offenses entailing expiation (*pācittiya*), inquiries concerning the twelve offenses entailing acknowledgment (*pāṭidesanīya*), inquiries concerning the offenses of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*), and inquiries concerning the offenses of improper speech (*dubbhāsita*).
"Inquiries concerning failure" refers to these.
Inquiries concerning failure in virtue, inquiries concerning failure in conduct, inquiries concerning failure in view, and inquiries concerning failure in livelihood.
Inquiries concerning offenses are:

inquiries concerning offenses entailing expulsion (*pārājika*), inquiries concerning offenses of formal meeting of the Saṅgha (*saṅghādisesa*), inquiries concerning grave offenses (*thullaccaya*), inquiries concerning offenses requiring expiation (*pācittiya*), inquiries concerning offenses to be confessed (*pāṭidesanīya*), inquiries concerning offenses of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*), and inquiries concerning offenses of improper speech (*dubbhāsita*).
"An inquiry concerning misconduct" means an inquiry concerning the attainment of the two-by-two union. "What have you seen? [is the question].
There are four kinds of questions: a question concerning characteristics, a question concerning modes of conduct, a question concerning manner, and a question concerning variation.
A question concerning characteristics is: "Is it long or short? Is it black or white?
A question concerning modes of conduct is: "Is it walking, standing, sitting, or lying down?"
"An inquiry regarding appearance" refers to whether one is in the appearance of a householder, the appearance of a member of another sect, or the appearance of one who has gone forth.
"An inquiry regarding behavior" refers to whether one is walking, standing, sitting, or lying down.
"When was it seen by you? [is the question.]
An inquiry regarding time, an inquiry regarding an occasion, an inquiry regarding the day, an inquiry regarding the season.
An inquiry regarding time means at the time of forenoon, or at the time of midday, or at the time of afternoon.
An inquiry regarding an occasion means at the occasion of forenoon, or at the occasion of midday, or at the occasion of afternoon.
"An inquiry about the day" means: before the meal, after the meal, at night, by day, during the dark fortnight, or during the bright fortnight.
"An inquiry about the season" means: in winter, summer, or the rainy season.
"Where have you seen it? means: where have you seen it?
A question concerning a place (*ṭhāna-pucchā*), a question concerning ground (*bhūmi-pucchā*), a question concerning space (*okāsa-pucchā*), and a question concerning a location (*padesa-pucchā*).
"A question concerning a place" refers to ground, earth, the world, or the world-system.
"A question concerning ground" refers to ground, earth, a mountain, a rock, or a palace.

"An inquiry regarding space" refers to the eastern space, the western space, the northern space, or the southern space. "An inquiry regarding location" refers to the eastern location, the western location, the northern location, or the southern location.
The *Mahāsaṅgāma* is concluded.
Its summary verse:
The basis, the origin, the mode,
the sequence, and what has been done or left undone.
The legal procedure concerning formal acts,
the settlement by means of consensus, and [the settlements] arising from desire,
hatred, delusion, and fear.
And by the manifestation of recognition;
I am one who has seen and gained confidence through those who are more senior in the Elder lineage and through those who have heard more.
That which has not been attained and that which has been attained,
according to the Dhamma and the Vinaya,
and also according to the Teacher’s instruction.
"Engaging in a great battle."
